title: Who will pay for Karnataka’s AI infrastructure bill? - Deccan Herald
full_text:
Karnataka has announced a Sustainable Data Centre Policy for 2026-2031 with a target of one gigawatt (GW) of cumulative data-centre IT load and 10-12% of India's AI-ready data-centre capacity by 2031. The policy focuses on renewable energy, efficient cooling, water management, and improved connectivity.
However, a new rule is required for the next phase of Bengaluru's digital evolution. Large data centres should have a public resource budget that indicates not only the efficiency of the facility, but also the extra strain it puts on local electricity and water supplies.
Operators can report an efficient power-usage ratio, enter into a renewable electricity contract or use advanced cooling technology. These are helpful indicators, but they don't answer a more local question: What will happen to the grid, water supply, and surrounding users when a large new load comes into a specific district?
A 1 GW goal is not just a technology-policy goal. Data centres are always on, demand reliable electricity supplies, and can generate concentrated demand where transmission capacity was not planned for it. They may consume considerable water depending on the cooling technology and climate. The true cost is, therefore, not just the operator's electricity bill. It can include substations, transmission lines, backup capacity, and local water infrastructure.
In August, the Union government informed Parliament that the environmental appraisal of qualifying data-centre projects takes into account freshwater availability, especially in water-stressed regions, as well as water balance, recycling, and reuse.
The United States now faces a similar issue as rapid data-centre growth has led to concerns about electricity costs and grid expansion. The US House passed a Bill on September 16 that would ask State regulators to determine whether very large electricity consumers should pay for infrastructure costs caused by their electricity use rather than existing households and businesses. The question is universal: Who pays for the infrastructure needed by the AI economy?
Karnataka can respond before the issue turns into a controversy.
There are four elements to a resource budget. First, the hourly electricity demand profile of a proposed facility. A data centre that can move some computing to off-peak times has a different system cost from one operating at maximum capacity.
Second, the operator should determine what new grid infrastructure is needed and make clear who will pay for it. The costs of a dedicated substation or transmission upgrade should not be passed on to ordinary consumers if that infrastructure is required primarily for a single large commercial customer.
Third, the budget should reveal water use by source and season. A facility that uses treated wastewater in the rainy season and potable municipal water in the dry season has a very different public impact from one that uses reclaimed water all year. Approval conditions should, therefore, be based on water sources rather than just litres.
Fourth, operators should make drought, heatwave, and grid-stress contingency plans public. What flexibility does a data centre provide if there is an electricity shortage or severe water constraint? Can non-urgent computing be moved to another place or time? These questions should be addressed before a crisis, not during one.
This reporting is not radical. The European Union requires significant data centres to report energy-performance and water-footprint information through a common database. Karnataka may go further and directly link this information with future approvals and incentives.
A resource budget would also incentivise developers to choose sites with a better grid, access to reclaimed water, and less environmental stress, instead of being drawn to Bengaluru only because of fibre, talent, and the corporate ecosystem.
Physical computing power is required for AI, cloud services, and digital public infrastructure. It's not data centres versus the environment. It's whether their underlying infrastructure expenses are accounted for before they become public expenses.
If Bengaluru or any other urban centre in Karnataka is to be the hub of the computing infrastructure of the future, each new megawatt should come with an answer to the question: what resources will it consume, what new infrastructure will it need, and who will pay for it?
A public resource budget would make that answer clear before the bill arrives.
Era Sakhuja is Deputy Programme Director of Emerging Technologies and Risk at the Centre for International Security and Economic Strategy (CISES) on a voluntary basis.

title: Worst drought in 150 years, 53 more taluks added to affected list in Karnataka - The New Indian Express
full_text:
BENGALURU: Karnataka has added another 53 taluks to its drought-hit list, taking the total number of drought-affected taluks in the state to 177, Deputy Chief Minister and Revenue Minister Dr G Parameshwara said on Tuesday.
He added that the number could rise to around 200 based on ground conditions and further assessment.
Speaking in the Legislative Council on Tuesday, Dr Parameshwara said the government was declaring drought-hit taluks strictly according to the drought declaration guidelines framed by the Union Government in 2020. He said the state had not witnessed a drought of such severity in the last 150 years.
Initially, 101 taluks were declared drought-hit, followed by another 23 after continued assessment. With the addition of 53 more taluks, the total has now reached 177. He said assessment would continue based on rainfall deficiency, crop damage and other prescribed parameters, while highlighting that the assessment was a continuous process.
The state normally receives around 852 mm of rainfall, but only 642 mm has been recorded, resulting in an average rainfall deficit of 36%. Severe rainfall deficits were reported in several regions during the period from June to September 26, he informed the House.
The deficit was 46% in South Interior Karnataka, 44% in North Interior Karnataka, 38% in Malnad and 28% in the coastal region.
Dr Parameshwara said the rainfall deficit had severely affected agriculture and farmers’ livelihoods. In several areas, farmers sowed crops when rains began, only for the rainfall to stop and the germinated crops to dry up. Some farmers sowed again after rains returned, but those crops too suffered damage.
He further said that due to the deficit the state has seen a 82% crop loss due to the super El Niño phenomenon, which has also contributed to the rainfall deficit.
Explaining the process of declaring drought-hit taluks, Parameshwara said declaring all taluks as drought-affected without meeting the prescribed criteria could create difficulties in securing relief from the Union Government.
“The Union Government must provide Karnataka the drought relief under those guidelines. At the same time, the state government will continue assessing the situation and ensuring relief reaches farmers,” he said.
Take Immediate Steps to Help Farmers: Sharavana
Bengaluru: JDS MLC T A Sharavana urged the government to act immediately on the prevailing drought situation in the state and address the hardships faced by farmers by taking up necessary relief measures. Speaking at the special session on Tuesday, the MLC said the drought situation is severe and is directly affecting the lives of farmers. The government should not limit itself to mere words on the plight of farmers but must take immediate and necessary relief measures, he said.
Speaking on farm loan waiver, Sharavana brought to the notice of the government that former Chief Minister and present Union Minister HD Kumaraswamy had waived farm loans to the tune of about Rs. 25,000 crore during his tenure as the CM.
He said there is a need for such firm and pro-farmer decisions without having to plead before the Central Government, and the present government too must take immediate steps to provide necessary assistance to farmers. He demanded that the State Government take an all-party delegation to the Centre to secure necessary assistance from the Central Government.
